tags.name: First visit
tags.description: Everything about coming for the first time: what we ask, what we do, and what it feels like.

posts.title: Autumn hours, and Saturday mornings from nine
posts.excerpt: From October the clinic opens at nine on Saturdays, with two first-visit openings every week and a quiet evening session on Fridays.
posts.content:
From the first Saturday of October we open an hour earlier, at nine. It began as an experiment in the summer, and so many of you took the early times that we are keeping them.

Each Saturday now has two first-visit openings, at 9:00 and 13:00, with Kei or Mio. The Friday evening session, our two-hour Quiet Evening, moves to 18:30 so you can come straight from work.

This season's hours

  • Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday — 10:00 to 19:30
  • Saturday — 9:00 to 16:00
  • Wednesday and Sunday — closed
  • 29 December to 3 January — closed for the new year

Nothing else changes: the same rooms, the same tea, the same three of us. If you have a standing appointment, it stays where it is.

posts.title: Why every first visit begins at the wrist
posts.excerpt: Three fingers on each wrist, a few quiet minutes, and the oldest way we know of noticing how someone is today.
posts.content:
Before any needle or moxa, we sit with you and rest three fingers on each wrist. It takes three or four minutes, and the room goes very quiet. People often ask what we are listening for.

The honest answer is: how you are today. Fast or slow, near the surface or deep, steady or a little uneven. It is not a medical test, and we never use it to tell anyone what illness they have. It is a way of paying close attention, the way a friend notices you look tired before you say so.

The pulse is where we stop talking and start listening.

Aoi Fujimori

What we notice shapes the treatment: which points, how many needles, whether warmth would help more than needles that day. Then, at the end of the hour, we take it again. Most people are surprised by how different it feels under their own fingers.

posts.title: Moxa at home for the cooling evenings
posts.excerpt: A gentle warmth for feet and lower back as the nights draw in: how our home-moxa lessons work, and three things to remember.
posts.content:
When the first cool evenings arrive, many people ask whether they can use moxa at home. Often they can, with a little teaching. Stick-on moxa with a small base, sold for home use, is simple and safe if you follow a few rules.

Mio teaches small groups of four on Saturday afternoons. In forty minutes you learn where to place the moxa, how warm it should feel and when to take it off, and you leave with a small kit.

Three things to remember

  • Warm, never hot: remove it the moment it feels too warm
  • Never on broken skin, or on areas without feeling
  • Open a window, sit still, and do not leave it alone

Home moxa is for comfort and relaxation. If you are pregnant, diabetic or unsure, ask us or your doctor first.

posts.title: Four minutes of breathing before sleep
posts.excerpt: In for four, out for six. The small practice we give to almost everyone at the end of a first visit.
posts.content:
At the end of most first visits we give the same small homework: four minutes of slow breathing in bed, lights out, phone in another room. It is so simple that people forget it works.

Lie on your back with one hand on your belly. Breathe in through the nose for a count of four, and out through the mouth, slowly, for a count of six. The out-breath is the important one. Let it be a little longer than feels natural.

  • Four minutes is enough; set a soft timer if it helps
  • If you lose count, start again at one without judging
  • Notice your shoulders sink a little on each out-breath

Many people tell us they are asleep before the four minutes are up. Some nights you will not be, and that is fine too: you have still spent four minutes resting.

posts.title: Mugwort, from the field to the moxa cone
posts.excerpt: Moxa is the soft wool of mugwort leaves, dried and sifted for months. A short history of the plant we burn every day.
posts.content:
Every cone of moxa begins as a mugwort leaf, a plant that grows along every riverbank and roadside here. Turn a leaf over and you see why it was chosen: the underside is covered in fine silver wool.

The leaves are picked in early summer, dried, then ground and sifted again and again until only the wool is left. The finest grade, pale and soft as cotton, takes the longest to make and burns the most gently.

Good moxa should feel like warm breath, not like a flame.

Mio Harada

In the clinic we use the fine grade for the tiny rice-grain cones, and a coarser one in the warming boxes for the back. If you would like to see and smell the difference, ask at your next visit.

posts.title: What a needle actually feels like
posts.excerpt: Thinner than you think, gentler than you fear. An honest account for anyone nervous about a first acupuncture visit.
posts.content:
Nerves about needles are the most common reason people put off a first visit. So here is an honest description, from people who have felt hundreds of them.

Our needles are about as thin as a hair and come individually packed, used once and thrown away. Each one goes in through a small guide tube with a light tap. Most of the time you feel the tap of the tube and nothing else.

What people tell us they feel

  • A dull heaviness or a mild ache around the point, for a moment
  • Warmth spreading slowly from the point
  • Very often, a sudden wish to sleep

If anything ever feels sharp, say so and the needle comes out at once. You are always in charge of the hour, and we will happily start with shiatsu or moxa instead.

posts.title: Wisteria week, and why the clinic has its name
posts.excerpt: For two weeks every spring the trellis outside our window flowers, and the waiting room smells of honey.
posts.content:
Fujinami means waves of wisteria, and for two weeks each spring the name makes sense. The trellis outside the second-floor window, older than the building, flowers in long pale clusters that move in the slightest wind.

We open the windows in both rooms during wisteria week. Lying on the treatment bed you can hear the bees, and many people tell us it is the most restful hour of their spring.

If you would like a time during next year's flowering, usually the last week of April, let us know: we keep a short list and write to you as the first buds open.

posts.title: Tea after treatment: why we always pour a cup
posts.excerpt: Roasted barley tea, a few quiet minutes and no rush to the door. The last step of every visit, and why it matters.
posts.content:
Every treatment here ends the same way: you sit up slowly, we pour a cup of warm roasted barley tea, and nobody hurries you to the door.

After an hour of rest the body is slow and warm, and stepping straight into a cold street can feel abrupt. Five minutes with a cup lets you come back gently. Barley tea has no caffeine, so it does not undo the quiet of the hour.

  • Drink something warm in the evening after a treatment
  • Go to bed a little earlier than usual that night
  • Skip hard exercise or a long hot bath until the next day

In winter we add a small sweet from the shop downstairs. It is not part of the treatment, strictly speaking, but nobody has ever complained.
